enrichment.short_title: Travelling show-people Green Belt injunction under section 187B

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Fairground operators unlawfully occupied a six-hectare Green Belt field at Platt, Kent, dividing it into 19 plots with caravans, heavy vehicles and fairground equipment.
Planning permission was refused, enforcement notices upheld, and the Secretary of State dismissed appeals while granting 12 months to vacate.

The council sought section 187B injunctive relief after the grace period expired; Stanley Burnton J granted the injunction despite evidence the appellants had nowhere else to go in South East England.
The appeal was heard after the House of Lords decision in South Bucks District Council v Porter on the court's independent discretion on enforcement and Article 8 proportionality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a High Court order granting a local planning authority an injunction under section 187B to restrain unlawful occupation of Green Belt land.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge properly exercised his discretion and the injunction was a proportionate response to deliberate and prolonged breach of planning control.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 187B application the court does not re-decide planning merits but must independently decide whether injunctive relief is just and proportionate, weighing hardship against the need to enforce planning control; deliberate unlawful occupation of environmentally sensitive land may outweigh Article 8 hardship even where no alternative site exists.
legal_issues: Whether the judge was unduly deferential to planning authority decisions on hardship and Article 8
Whether refusal of injunctive relief would effectively grant temporary planning permission
Whether alternative enforcement by self-help or criminal prosecution should have been preferred
Whether eviction was a disproportionate interference with Article 8 rights
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter [2003] 2 WLR 1547
Chapman v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 399
Wrexham CBC v Berry [2003] EWCA Civ 835

enrichment.short_title: Entitlement to compensation after quashed stop notice at Shoreham

statutes_considered.title: Harbours, Docks and Piers Clauses Act 1847

key_facts: International Traders Ferry used Shoreham Harbour in 1994-95 to export live animals under port licences from the Shoreham Port Authority.
Adur District Council served an enforcement notice and stop notice; the enforcement notice was later quashed on appeal because the use was held not to breach planning control.
ITF claimed compensation under section 186 but the Lands Tribunal held it had neither an interest in nor occupation of the land on the date the stop notice was served.
ITF's February 1998 letter was held to constitute a valid compensation claim, but the entitlement preliminary issue failed for lack of interest or occupation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Lands Tribunal preliminary issues on entitlement to section 186 compensation and validity of the compensation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; ITF had no legal or equitable interest and was not an occupier for section 186 purposes, though its letter was a valid claim.
enrichment.ratio: Section 186 compensation requires a legal or equitable interest or occupation with sufficient permanence and control at the date the stop notice is served; non-exclusive port licences subject to harbour-master direction do not confer such interest or occupation, and Pennine Raceway is distinguishable because section 186 uses the narrower phrase 'interest in' land.
legal_issues: Whether ITF had an interest in land under section 186(2)
Whether ITF occupied part of the port despite licence conditions
Whether the February 1998 letter satisfied Regulation 12
Whether Article 1 Protocol 1 affected construction of interest or occupy
linked_authorities: Pennine Raceway v Kirklees MBC [1983] 1 QB 382
Stevens v Bromley London Borough Council [1972] 1 Ch 400
Horn v Sunderland Corporation [1941] 2 KB 26
Tre Traktorer Aktiebolag v Sweden (1989) 13 EHRR 309

enrichment.short_title: Bench saw injury: employer liability despite experienced joiner

statutes_considered.title: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999
Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998

key_facts: An experienced joiner lost his thumb and index finger using a portable bench saw supplied by Chester City Council while trimming long fascia boards without a run-off bench or assistant.
The trial judge rejected the claimant's account of how the accident happened and held the employer's admitted regulatory breaches were not causative.
Experts agreed a risk assessment should have identified the need for support when cutting flexible 5-metre boards on a short bench.
The employer had provided the saw on request but gave no training, risk assessment or instruction on safe use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against dismissal of an employers' liability claim after trial on liability only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; employers were negligent and in breach of statutory duty, causative of the accident, with contributory negligence assessed at 60%.
enrichment.ratio: Even skilled employees are entitled to a safe system of work and identification of obvious risks through risk assessment or instruction; where lack of a run-off bench or second worker was an obvious requirement and the employer failed to address it, employer fault is not co-extensive with the employee's own failure and damages may be reduced for conscious risk-taking.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately addressed common law duty and causation
Whether admitted breaches of PUWER and manual handling regulations were causative
Whether Ginty v Belmont excluded liability where the employee knew the precaution required
Apportionment of contributory negligence in breach of statutory duty cases
linked_authorities: Ginty v Belmont Building Ltd [1959] 1 All ER 414
Boyle v Kodak Ltd [1969] 2 All ER 439
Reeves v Commissioner of Metropolitan Police [2000] 1 AC 360
Toole v Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council [2002] EWCA Civ 588

enrichment.short_title: NASS support during out-of-time IAT permission application
key_facts: A Turkish Kurd asylum seeker lost an adjudicator appeal promulgated in October 2003 and sought permission to appeal to the IAT.
Her application notice was posted by special delivery on 16 October 2003 but received on 20 October 2003 because of industrial action, missing the 10-day deadline.
NASS discontinued section 95 support on 28 October 2003 on the basis the appeal was finally determined, despite the outstanding permission application.
By February 2004 the IAT had still not determined the out-of-time permission application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of withdrawal of asylum support pending determination of an out-of-time application for permission to appeal to the IAT.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; quashing order made; the claimant remained an asylum-seeker with a pending appeal when the IAT received her application; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal under section 82 is instituted and pending under section 104(2)(a) once an application for permission to appeal is received by the IAT, even if an extension of time is required; section 104(2)(b) does not treat such an application as finally determined merely because the permission deadline has passed.

Whether an out-of-time permission application is an instituted appeal under section 104(2)(a)

Whether support should continue while IAT permission is undetermined

enrichment.short_title: Murder-house sale: honest 'no' on SPIF question 13
key_facts: Buyers purchased 16 Stillwell Drive, Wakefield, unaware it had been the scene of a gruesome murder and dismemberment by a former occupier.

Sellers learned of the history from anonymous press cuttings in March 1999, took legal advice that no duty to disclose arose, and answered 'no' to question 13 of the Seller's Property Information Form when selling in 2000.
After a Channel 5 documentary in July 2001 the buyers discovered the history, could not live in the house, and resold at a substantial discount.
The judge held there was no general duty to disclose the murder and that question 13 required only an honest subjective answer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from trial of liability issues in a conveyancing misrepresentation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; no misrepresentation or negligence where question 13 was answered honestly; costs order on cross-appeal upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Question 13 of the Law Society Seller's Property Information Form asks whether the vendor honestly believes there is other information the buyer may have a right to know; it does not import an objective reasonable-grounds test or extend caveat emptor to require disclosure of heinous but non-defective historical facts.
legal_issues: Whether vendors owed a duty to disclose the property's murder history
Construction of SPIF question 13 as subjective or objective
Whether an honest 'no' could amount to misrepresentation or negligent misstatement
Whether the judge's split costs order was wrong
linked_authorities: Economides v Commercial Assurance Co Plc [1998] QB 587
William Sindall Plc v Cambridgeshire County Council [1994] 1 WLR 1016

enrichment.short_title: GDC suspension: adequacy of PCC reasons for dishonesty finding
key_facts: Dr Luthra was suspended for six months by the GDC Professional Conduct Committee for dishonestly submitting false NHS Dental Practice Board claims relating to three patients in 1997-1999.
He admitted many factual allegations but denied dishonest intent, attributing errors to incompetence or administrative mistakes.
On appeal under section 29 he abandoned original grounds and relied on inadequate reasons and Article 6 unfairness.
The panel found dishonesty on eight teeth under Code 1444 and on other claims, leading to serious professional misconduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 29 of the Dental Act 1984 against a GDC suspension for serious professional misconduct.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to rely on fresh grounds refused; panel reasons adequate for credibility-based dishonesty findings; costs awarded to the GDC.
enrichment.ratio: Professional conduct committees need not give detailed reasons for preferring prosecution evidence over a registrant's account where the dispute turns on credibility; specific findings on each charge suffice unless fairness requires more, following Selvanathan and Gupta; suspension took effect on dismissal of the appeal under section 30.
legal_issues: Whether the PCC gave adequate reasons for dishonesty findings
Whether failure to give reasons breached natural justice or Article 6
Whether technical dental coding disputes required fuller reasoning
Whether the court could stay suspension pending further appeal
linked_authorities: Selvanathan v General Medical Council [2001] Lloyd's Rep Med 1
Gupta v General Medical Council [2001] UKPC 61
Ghosh v General Medical Council [2001] 1 WLR 1915

enrichment.short_title: Second construction adjudication not enforced for bias

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Amec claimed £508,401.52 from Whitefriars under a JCT design-and-build letter of intent after pre-construction works were terminated in 2001.
Adjudicator Michael Biscoe awarded Amec in a first adjudication, but enforcement failed because the contract named George Ashworth as adjudicator and Biscoe lacked jurisdiction.
After Geoffrey Ashworth's death and a Rockwater revocation action, Amec commenced a second adjudication and Biscoe was re-nominated by the RIBA.
Biscoe again awarded Amec £597,371.78; Whitefriars resisted enforcement on jurisdiction, bias and natural justice grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 application to enforce a second construction adjudication award under section 108(5).
enrichment.outcome: Enforcement refused; although Scheme appointment issues favoured Amec on misnomer, overall bias and natural justice failures invalidated the award; Whitefriars awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: Re-appointment of an adjudicator who decided the same dispute, use of undisclosed legal advice from the first adjudication on withholding notices, deciding jurisdiction before disclosing Clyde & Co advice, and an ex parte telephone call with the referring party's solicitor created a real possibility of bias; undisclosed expert legal advice on merits or jurisdiction breaches natural justice.

Whether George Ashworth was a misnomer for Geoffrey Ashworth
Whether re-appointment of the same adjudicator gave rise to apparent bias

enrichment.short_title: Russian privatisation advice: loss-of-chance reduced to 40%
key_facts: IML acquired 49% of Russian suit manufacturer Bolshevichka in 1993 relying on Coudert Brothers for local law advice on privatisation documents.
GKI had approved a three-year investment plan but IML's tender and agreements contemplated five-year investment; Russian courts later invalidated the transaction on that basis.
After Coudert's negligent failure to identify the three-year plan, IML lost its investment when the Moscow prosecutor challenged the deal in 1996.
The judge found negligence and assessed recoverable chance at 70%; Coudert appealed on causation, estoppel and anti-monopoly grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against High Court findings of solicitors' negligence and 70% loss-of-chance assessment in a Russian privatisation claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; loss-of-chance reduced from 70% to 40%; anti-monopoly point could not break causation as defendant's own fault; three-year plan finding upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors' negligence causing loss of a commercial chance is recoverable under Allied Maples where hypothetical third-party conduct is assessed as a percentage chance; a defendant cannot rely on its own later negligence to break causation of that lost chance, and upgrading the chance for improbability of prosecution overlooked the Gurov influence that downgraded it.
legal_issues: Whether the claim was loss of chance or all-or-nothing causation
Whether GKI approved a three-year or five-year investment plan
Whether anti-monopoly approval failure was an independent cause barring recovery
Whether Coudert could rely on its own fault on the anti-monopoly point
Whether 70% was the correct loss-of-chance assessment
linked_authorities: Allied Maples Group Ltd v Simmons & Simmons [1995] 4 All ER 907
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 1 AC 1
Goode v Martin [2001] EWCA Civ 1899

enrichment.short_title: Patent inquiry damages despite later revocation by third party
key_facts: Coflexip obtained judgment for infringement of EP(UK) 0478742 against Stolt and an inquiry as to damages for seabed conduit-laying technology.
Stolt did not rely on prior art Recalde at trial; Rockwater later revoked the patent on that art in separate proceedings.
Stolt applied to stay the inquiry and rely on revocation as a complete defence, invoking Poulton v Adjustable Cover.
The inquiry could involve about £80 million across 15 contracts using the same vessel and process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to stay a patent inquiry as to damages after later third-party revocation of the patent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; Stolt estopped from relying on later revocation at the inquiry; no stay ordered pending Rockwater appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where validity and subsistence of a patent were finally determined between the same parties, issue estoppel prevents a later revocation obtained by a third party from being relied on at an inquiry as to damages unless the invalidating prior art could not have been found with reasonable diligence; Poulton remains binding and Johnson v Gore Wood does not permit reopening decided validity in the same action.
legal_issues: Whether Stolt was estopped from relying on Rockwater revocation at the inquiry
Whether Poulton v Adjustable Cover remained good law after the Patents Act 1977
Cause of action versus issue estoppel across multiple infringing contracts
Whether section 130(7) imported CPC Article 33 revocation effects
Whether the inquiry should be stayed pending parallel appeals
linked_authorities: Poulton v Adjustable Cover and Boiler Block Co [1908] 2 Ch 430
Arnold v National Westminster Bank plc [1991] 2 AC 93

enrichment.short_title: Coroner costs after Article 2 inquest judicial review
key_facts: Following the court's merits judgment of 2 December 2003 in R (Davies) v HM Deputy Coroner for Birmingham, the parties argued costs on 14 January 2004.
The legally aided claimant sought costs against the deputy coroner at first instance and on appeal, relying on R (Touche) v Inner North London Coroner.
The court reviewed long-standing practice on costs orders against inferior courts and tribunals that actively contest judicial review.
Brooke LJ affirmed Touche in part but distinguished cases where a coroner assists neutrally rather than as a contesting party.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs submissions after successful judicial review appeal concerning coroner's Article 2 inquest duties.
enrichment.outcome: Deputy coroner ordered to pay the claimant's costs of the Court of Appeal only; no order disturbing costs below in the coroner's favour at first instance.
enrichment.ratio: A coroner who actively contests judicial review becomes a party at risk on costs if unsuccessful on appeal, but need not pay first-instance costs where the law had not yet moved against him; neutral affidavit-only participation avoids adverse costs, though Touche supports costs against active resistance where no other public funding exists.
legal_issues: When an inferior court or tribunal should pay judicial review costs
Distinction between contesting party and neutral amicus roles
Effect of R (Touche) on coroners' costs liability
Whether CPR and Article 2 considerations alter historic Divisional Court practice
